claims.text: Machine-learning-optimized low-energy laser powder bed fusion can reduce thermal gradients in AlCrFeNiSi feedstock.
Reducing thermal gradients will decrease residual stresses in the fabricated components.
The proposed regime will improve microstructural uniformity and restore mechanical properties relative to high-thermal-load processing.
The AlCrFeNiSi feedstock has typical additive-manufacturing particle morphology and composition.
A material-agnostic machine-learning method can identify laser powder bed fusion process conditions.
The machine-learning method can specifically select a low-energy condition using lower laser power and higher scanning speed.
Lower laser power and higher scanning speed minimize thermal gradients in AlCrFeNiSi.
Machine-learning-selected process parameters can produce laser powder bed fusion products with greater than 98% relative density.
The greater-than-98% relative-density result is applicable to AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
The proposed process is applicable to AlCrFeNiSi components with characteristic dimensions of 1–5 mm under ambient processing conditions.
Lower energy input decreases melt-pool dimensions.
Decreased melt-pool dimensions and reduced thermal gradients produce quenching that limits grain growth.
The proposed quenching process limits phase segregation.
Limited grain growth and phase segregation decrease residual stress.
A finer and more homogeneous microstructure improves mechanical properties.
The optimized low-energy regime will yield significantly lower X-ray-diffraction-measured residual stress than conventional high-thermal-load processing.
The optimized low-energy regime will yield a finer and more uniform SEM/EBSD-observed microstructure.
The optimized low-energy regime will increase tensile strength and ductility relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing.
Conventional high-energy laser powder bed fusion typically causes high residual stress, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity due to extensive melt-pool dynamics.
The machine-learning approach has been experimentally validated for high relative density using 316L stainless steel, AlSi10Mg, and Fe60Co15Ni15Cr10 powders.
